The electric eel Electrophorus electricus demonstrates a remarkable capacity for survival in the oxygen-poor waters of the Amazon and Orinoco basins, a feat enabled by its obligate air-breathing behavior. At hatching, the prolarvae are remarkably small, measuring just 0.9 cm  in total length, a size that reflects their lecithotrophic, non-feeding stage. Yolk absorption is rapid under captive conditions maintained at a stable water temperature of 25.5 °C [T = 25.5 °C], with the first exogenous feeding usually observed around 19 days after hatching. At this critical trophic switch, the young-of-year have reached a total length of 3.5 cm , marking the transition from endotrophic to exotrophic nutrition at a temperature of 25.5 °C [T = 25.5 °C]. The acceleration of somatic growth during this early juvenile phase is pronounced, and by 61 days post-hatch, individuals commonly attain a length of 8 cm , though this trajectory is highly dependent on the availability of suitably small prey items such as insect larvae and crustaceans at a temperature of 25.5 °C [T = 25.5 °C].

Sexual maturation in this species is a protracted process that occurs under the same thermal regime near 25.5 °C [T = 25.5 °C] that governs early development. The initiation of gametogenesis and the onset of gonadal recrudescence are not evident until individuals have passed through an extended pre-reproductive juvenile stage. The age at first reproduction, or first spawning event, has been estimated from long-term captive records at approximately 1,095 days after hatching [tR = approximately 1,095 days after hatching] at a temperature of 25.5 °C [T = 25.5 °C]. At this pivotal life-history transition, the breeding individual measures about 68.5 cm [Lp = about 68.5 cm] in total length, a size that corresponds to a wet body weight of about 782 grams [Wwp = about 782 grams]. These values are notably conservative for a gymnotiform of this ultimate potential; for instance, the same cohort reaches a much greater size at the completion of growth.

The maximal lifespan of the electric eel has been inferred from both field mark-recapture studies and long-term aquarium husbandry data. Records indicate that individuals can survive for up to 22 years [am = up to 22 years] in captivity when water temperatures remain near 25 °C [T = 25 °C], though senescent adults in the wild likely experience higher rates of natural mortality due to increased vulnerability to predation and diminishing foraging efficiency. This relatively lengthy lifespan is accompanied by an extraordinary capacity for asymptotic growth. The ultimate total length achieved by the largest sexually mature adults has been documented at 250 cm [Li = 250 cm], a figure that is among the highest recorded for any freshwater teleost. Correspondingly, the ultimate wet weight attained by these reproductively active adults can approach 20,000 grams [Wwi = 20,000 grams], reflecting a massive investment in somatic tissue that supports their high-voltage electrogenic capabilities.

Reproductive output in the electric eel is notable for its comparatively modest fecundity given the species' large body size. Females produce, on average, 46 to 47 eggs per clutch [N_R_i = 46 to 47 eggs per clutch] during each spawning event, a number that is low relative to many other large-bodied gymnotiforms. The frequency of these spawning events, however, is surprisingly high; a single gravid female can produce approximately one clutch per year [F_R_i = approximately one clutch per year] under optimal captive conditions near 25 °C [T = 25 °C]. This annual reproductive effort yields a modest daily reproductive rate when averaged across the lifespan, but the extended longevity of the species--spanning up to 22 years [am = up to 22 years]--allows for substantial cumulative lifetime fecundity, a pattern consistent with an iteroparous life-history strategy that buffers against environmental stochasticity in floodplain nursery ha at a temperature of 25 °C [T = 25 °C]bitats.

Remarkable variation in growth trajectory is observed across the first several months of life, with animals reared at 25.5 °C [T = 25.5 °C] demonstrating a clear inflection point in their length-at-age relationship. While the early larval stages proceed at a moderate pace, with hatching occurring after just 9 days  of incubation and a hatchling birth length of 1.9 cm [Lb = 1.9 cm], a dramatic acceleration in growth occurs after the transition to exogenous feeding at a temperature of 25.5 °C [T = 25.5 °C]. By 195 days post-hatch, captive juveniles reared under these stable thermal conditions have reached a total length of 70 cm , representing an approximately twentyfold increase in length from the initial hatchling size of 0.9 cm  at a temperature of 25.5 °C [T = 25.5 °C]. This rapid juvenile growth phase is critical for escaping gape-limited predation and for developing the powerful electric organs necessary for both prey detection and defense, ultimately enabling these young fish to achieve the substantial size required for reproductive maturation around 68.5 cm [Lp = around 68.5 cm] and a wet weight of about 782 grams [Wwp = about 782 grams].
